/-əns/ Suffix Added to an adjective or verb to form a noun indicating a state or condition, such as result or capacity, associated with the verb. Added to a verb to form a noun indicating a process or action. Usage Note Many words ending in "-ance" were formed in French or by alteration of a noun or adjective ending in "-ant". From Middle English -aunce , -ance , from Anglo-Norman -aunce and continental Old French -ance , from Latin -ant- , -ent- + -ia , from stem of Latin -āns , -ēns .
Suffix Used to make adjectives corresponding to nouns ending in -cide .
Suffix Combining form denoting years. From Latin -enniālis , from annus + -ium + -ālis .
Suffix ( soil science ) Any inceptisol with clearly defined characteristics. Clipping of (inc)ept(isol) .

Suffix Used to form diminutives, loosely construed. Synonyms: ( suffixes ) -cule, -ee, -el, -ette, -icle, -ie, -kin, -le, -let, -ling, -ole, -ule, -y, ( prefixes ) mini-, micro-, nano- Used to augment verbs, largely monosyllabic, to form verbs with a frequentative or imitative force. Inherited from Middle English -et , from Old French -et , from Late Latin -ittus , -ettus . Uncertain. Perhaps ultimately related to Middle English -ten , -eten , from Old English -ettan ; possibly reinforced by Old...
/fuː/ Suffix ( slang ) Used to form nouns indicating expertise or mastery of specified skill or area of knowledge. Back-formation from kung fu .

Usage Note In current usage, only standard for forming nouns (e.g., cheerfull is now a misspelling). For nouns, both forms have historically been considered acceptable; e.g., Weld’s Progressive English Grammar provides both spoonful and bowl-full as examples. Now usually hyphenated (e.g., bowl-full instead of bowlfull ), though both the spelling -ful and spaced compounds with full are more common (e.g., bowl full ); however, the plural is rarely formed by suffixing -s instead of pluralizing the ...

/aɪ/, /iː/ Suffix Used to form adjectives, nouns, demonyms (describing people of a particular city, region or country) or genonyms (describing people of a particular tribe, clan or family) and the language spoken by these people. Forms an alternative plural ending for various words borrowed from Latin that end in ⟨us⟩ in the singular. (nonstandard, sometimes proscribed) Forms an alternative plural ending for various words that end in ⟨us⟩ in the singular, despite not being borrowed from ...

/ɪsɪzem/ Suffix Forms abstract nouns from Greek or Latin bases. From -ic +‎ -ism , either based directly on the adjective in -ic (as in asceticism , mysticism ), or on the verb in -ise (as in anglicism ). Some productivity within English, as in witticism (1670s, by analogy with criticism ).
Suffix indicates a female variant of a noun ending in -ian Borrowed from French -ienne , feminine of -ien (“-ian”).
Suffix Used to form names of numerical bases (radixes). Rebracketing of decimal , as if it were from dec- +‎ -imal .
Suffix Synonym of -logy (“branch of learning; a study of a particular subject”). Synonyms: -ics, -logy, -s
Suffix Forms adjectives denoting "pertaining to, characterized by, having the nature of, resembling, tending to." From Latin -ītius or -īcius .
Suffix superlative form of -ly : most -ly

/ˈlɒ.d͡ʒə.kəl/, /ˈlɒ.d͡ʒɪ.kəl/ Suffix Used to form adjectival forms of nouns ending in -logy . Usage Note Relatively few terms are directly derived using this suffix. Terms ending in logical are often derived from words formed in other languages or by suffixing -ical to a word ending in logy , as biological = biology + -ical and genealogical = genealogy + -ical .
Infix ( pharmacology ) a monoclonal antibody that targets mammary tumors From mammary .

/-mə.tə/, /-mɪ.tə/, /-mɪ.təɹ/, /-mɪ.təɾ/, /-mɪ.ʈəɾ/, /-mɪ.ʈɜː(ɾ)/ Suffix Used to form the names of measuring devices. Usage Note Whereas the spelling of the unit of length varies between British ( metre ) and American ( meter ) English, the spelling of this suffix is -meter in both, while -metre is a nonstandard alternative form found in British English. Words with the suffix - o meter (compare -o- ) always have a primary stress on the antepenultimate syllable: ba rom eter , speed om eter , ta c...
Suffix ( organic chemistry ) used to form the names of carboxylic groups and acids Clipped from benzoic.
/ə.ləʊn/, /əˌloʊn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of steroids or steroidlike drugs that are not prednisolone derivatives.
Infix ( pharmacology ) a monoclonal antibody that targets bone From Latin os (“bone”).
/ˈpɛɹ.ɪ.nʌks/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of synthetic heparinoids. From -parin (“heparin derivative”).

Suffix ( medicine ) Forms nouns describing a condition related to production of voice or reaction to sound. Learned borrowing from Classical Latin -phōnia , from Ancient Greek -φωνία (-phōnía). By surface analysis, -phone +‎ -ia . Doublet of -phony .

/pəl/ Suffix ( as a noun ) A tuple containing the specified number of terms. ( as an adjective ) Containing the specified number of terms. From Latin -plus (“more, in sum”). From Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis).
/-plɛks/ Suffix Comprising a number of parts, as in duplex . ( mathematics ) ten to the power of the number, as in googolplex .
Suffix Used to form intensified adjectives from nouns and adjectives. Synonym: -riffic Back-formation from terrific .
/ɹɪn.əʊn/, /ɹɪˌnoʊn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of amrinone derivatives used as cardiac stimulants. From amrinone .

/-sɔːs/ Suffix ( slang ) Used to add emphasis to adjectives, especially those that relate to cool- or uncoolness. Usage Note Sometimes written with a space or a dash. Probably a back-formation from awesome sauce .
Suffix Misspelling of -saurus .
/səˌmaɪd/, /sɪm.ʌɪd/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of furosemide derivatives used as diuretics. From furosemide .

/sə.tɹɒn/, /səˌtɹɑn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of serotonin receptor 5-HT 3 antagonists not fitting into other established groups of serotonin receptor antagonists. Blend of se(ro)t(onin) receptor +‎ antagon(ist) .

Suffix ( fandom slang ) Added to a noun to describe a character of the noun's form, typically one used to represent oneself in fandom spaces. ( by extension ) Added to a noun to indicate a separate presentation of the self used in a certain real life context. Likely originated in the furry community with fursona . See also sona .
/-staɪn/, /-stiːn/ Suffix Added to a stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname. Usage Note Along with -berg and -witz, -stein is a common Ashkenazi suffix. Borrowed from German -stein .
/ˈtaɪ.ɹəl.ɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of thyrotropin-releasing hormone analogs. From thy(rotropin) +‎ -relin (“pituitary hormone release–stimulating peptide”).
